questions.q: What does UNPIVOT do relative to PIVOT?
options: The identical operation, just with different syntax
Adds an aggregate function to a PIVOT result
The exact opposite — turns several columns back into rows
Removes duplicate rows, unrelated to PIVOT
questions.explain: PIVOT goes rows-to-columns; UNPIVOT goes columns-to-rows.

questions.q: In the QuarterlySales example, what do the four Q1Sales-Q4Sales columns become after UNPIVOT?
options: A single combined column with all four values concatenated together
Four separate tables
They remain unchanged — UNPIVOT only affects row count, not columns
Two columns — Quarter (which column it came from) and SalesAmount (the value) — with one row per original column
questions.explain: This is the tall-shape result: one row per SalesID per quarter, instead of one row per SalesID with four quarter columns.

questions.q: Does UNPIVOT require an aggregate function, like PIVOT does?
options: Only when combined with GROUP BY
Yes, UNPIVOT requires the same aggregate function as PIVOT
UNPIVOT requires two aggregate functions
No — UNPIVOT is just reshaping, with no aggregation involved
questions.explain: This is one of the syntax differences between the two — PIVOT summarizes with an aggregate, UNPIVOT just restructures.

questions.q: What kind of real-world data typically needs UNPIVOT applied to it?
options: Data that arrives already 'wide' (like a spreadsheet import) and needs to be normalized into a tall shape for proper querying
Data that is already normalized and in a tall shape
Data with no NULL values anywhere
Only data stored in VARCHAR(MAX) columns
questions.explain: Spreadsheet-style exports or legacy system data with one column per category are the classic UNPIVOT candidates.

questions.q: In UNPIVOT's syntax, what does FOR name?
options: The WHERE condition applied afterward
The new column that holds which original column each row came from
The aggregate function used to summarize values
The table being unpivoted
questions.explain: This mirrors PIVOT's FOR clause, but in the reverse direction — it names the column, not creates new columns.
